title: Kirat karo, deeper
hook: honest work as spiritual practice, not only income

segments.voice: Yesterday the Var in Majh closed with another's right: pork to one neighbor, beef to the other. Your line was live up to your name. Did you leave what wasn't yours where it belonged? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

Sawdust on the forearms. A plane sliding along a board, curls of wood dropping to the floor. Somewhere in Punjab, the story goes, a carpenter named Lalo worked like this all day, and a rich official named Malik Bhago threw a great feast down the road. Guru Nanak was invited to the feast. He ate the carpenter's plain bread instead. When the official demanded to know why, the story says, Nanak took a piece of bread from each table and squeezed. From Lalo's came milk. From the feast came blood. It's a story Sikhs tell, not a line from the Granth. But it asks a sharp question, and it's today's question. What is the work of your hands actually made of?
screen: `A CARPENTER'S BREAD.` → `A RICH MAN'S FEAST.` → `MILK, AND BLOOD.`

segments.voice: One Sikh summary of Guru Nanak's way has three short phrases: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn by honest work; vand chhako, share what you have. We've met them before. This week we go deeper, one at a time, and we start with work. Kirat means labor, the work of your own effort. Karo means do it. Here's the line in the Granth that sits under it, from a salok of Guru Nanak, in paraphrase. Someone who calls himself a guru or a holy man and goes about begging: don't bow at his feet. The one who eats what he has earned by his own effort, and gives some of it from his hand, Nanak says, that one recognizes the path. Look at what that salok puts together. Holiness isn't proven by leaving work behind. In this line, the one who has found the way is someone with a paycheck, or a harvest, or a till at the end of the day, and something in their hand to give. Earning and the path aren't two rooms. They're the same room. That's why the Lalo story lands. It isn't a story against wealth. It's a story about where the bread came from. Bread made by honest hands carries something good. Bread made by squeezing other people carries what was squeezed. So kirat is more than having a job. It's how the job is done. The honest invoice. The full hour for the full wage. The repair done right when nobody would have noticed. Done that way, the work itself becomes part of the practice, not a break from it. That's today's line.
screen: `THREE PHRASES, ONE WAY.` · `KIRAT: THE WORK OF YOUR OWN EFFORT.` · `EARN, AND GIVE FROM THE HAND.` · `HOW THE JOB IS DONE.` · then, large: `WORK AS PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: work one hour as prayer. In the sit, choose the hour. It could be the next hour of your job, an hour of cooking, cleaning, study, or caring for someone. Picture yourself starting it. Now set one intention for that hour: honest, whole, done well, nobody watching required. Breathe slowly and let your hands rest open on your knees, the hands that will do the work. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kirat karo. Earn by honest work, the labor of your own effort, done in a way that is itself part of the spiritual life. Today's word.
Your line: work as prayer. Keep the hour you chose. When it ends, notice one thing you did more honestly than you would have otherwise. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karo as earning a living honestly by their own effort, and Sikh teachers describe daily work, done truthfully, as part of a Sikh life rather than apart from it.

match.prompt: the three phrases: tap the pairs.
pairs: the carpenter whose bread Nanak ate

myth: in the salok, the one who gives up work and begs is the holy one
the salok says don't bow to the self-styled holy man who begs; the one who earns and gives recognizes the path.
the milk-and-blood bread is a story Sikhs tell, not a line in the Granth
it's a story about Lalo and Malik Bhago; the Granth line is the salok about earning and giving.
kirat karo is only about having a job
it's about how the work is done: honestly, by your own effort, with something to give.

fork.setup: a carpenter offers plain bread. a rich official offers a feast. you are Guru Nanak. where do you eat?
options: at the feast, to honor the official.
fork.reveal: the story says he ate Lalo's bread, and when pressed, showed milk in it and blood in the feast's.

original.note: kirat is labor, the work of your own effort; karo means do it.

trapdoor: what you thought: kirat karo just means have a job.
what it means: earn by your own honest effort, so the work itself is part of the practice.
what a scholar hears: the salok pairs eating what you earn by effort with giving from the hand, and says that one recognizes the path.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Sarang ki Var, salok Mahala 1, Ang 1245 (one who eats what he earns by effort and gives something from his hand recognizes the path)
